network.overall_strategy: Construct ten operationally distinct, literature-supported precursor-to-aspartate pathways: six reductive-amination implementations, two metal-assisted transaminations, the malonate–glyoxylate route, and a cyanide/Bucherer–Bergs route. Catalyst-specific alternatives are counted explicitly; these are not ten independent mechanistic families. Oxaloacetate, glyoxylate, malonate, hydroxylamine and pyridoxamine are declared supplied inventories where required. Their continuous production from inorganic carbon is not established or silently assumed. The graph represents chemical identities shared between alternative compartments, not a demonstrated one-pot environmental network. Cyanide chemistry, metal/H2 chemistry and transamination operate separately; no physical pooling or cyanide–metal compatibility is assumed. Reported operating conditions and yields are distinguished from proposed engineering conditions wherever the supplied research lacks a complete protocol. Organic acids are represented using neutral reference formulas, while the target is standardized as net-minus-one aspartate after equilibration near pH 7–8. Explicit hydrogen ions represent buffer exchange rather than acidic conditions in alkaline experiments. Iron(II) is an oxidation-state bookkeeping product; its subsequent complexation and precipitation are not resolved. Products are expected to be racemic unless demonstrated otherwise. Oxaloacetate decarboxylation and competing carbonyl reduction are included, and no sustained environmental productivity is claimed without kinetic measurements.

reactions.name: Oxaloacetate reductive amination by partially electroreduced FeS containing Fe(0)
agents: Partially electroreduced FeS scaffold containing nanoscopic Fe(0); Fe(0) is a consumed reductant

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm under an inert atmosphere
conditions.catalyst: FeS-supported electron-transfer interface; not untreated FeS
conditions.other: Reported benchmark: 5 mM oxaloacetate, 0.5 M ammonia, pH 9.6, 48 h. The active solid was prepared separately at −0.7 V versus SHE for seven days; amination proceeded without continued electrolysis. Use a cool, anoxic mineral-interface compartment and freshly supplied oxaloacetate. Do not expose this compartment to cyanide or assume that bulk-ocean ammonia reaches the experimental concentration. Fe(II) may become sorbed or precipitated rather than remain freely dissolved.

reactions.mechanism: Oxaloacetate and ammonia form an imine/iminium ensemble. Oxidation of embedded Fe(0) supplies the two-electron reduction that produces the amino-acid skeleton. The sulfide interface facilitates adsorption and electron transfer.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) reported 64% aspartate under these substrate, pH, temperature and residence-time conditions. This is an experimental precursor-conversion yield, not an environmental yield. Ordinary FeS was much less effective, so the specified reduction state is essential. The authors did not obtain organic feedstocks directly from CO2 with this material under their tested conditions. Natural generation of the active surface, sufficient ammonia concentration and competition with rxn_014 remain independent requirements.

reactions.name: Oxaloacetate reductive amination by unsupported metallic iron
agents: Unpassivated Fe(0) surface; stoichiometric electron donor

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm under an inert atmosphere
conditions.other: Proposed matched comparison with rxn_001: 5 mM oxaloacetate, 0.5 M total ammoniacal nitrogen, pH 9.6, sampled through 48 h. These numerical settings define the comparison rather than a separately verified optimum for unsupported iron. Supply at least the stoichiometric Fe(0) electron inventory, with excess and accessible surface area determined experimentally. Track passivation, dissolved/solid Fe(II), pyruvate and aspartate.

reactions.mechanism: An oxaloacetate-derived imine is reduced by oxidation of exposed Fe(0). Unlike rxn_001, there is no sulfide scaffold controlling adsorption or electron transfer.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) directly found aspartate formation with pure Fe(0), but with poorer selectivity because oxaloacetate decarboxylation generated pyruvate and subsequently alanine. This is therefore a supported catalyst-material alternative, not an assumed equivalent of FeS_PERM. The stated matched operating window is a proposed implementation; no 64% yield is transferred to this branch. Native iron availability, corrosion and surface passivation constrain geological performance.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination over supported nickel

conditions.catalyst: Ni/SiO2–Al2O3, 10 mol% Ni relative to ketoacid
conditions.other: Reported standard platform: 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 h. For this substrate loading, five equivalents corresponds to 150 mM ammonium bicarbonate. Ammonia/ammonium and carbonate speciation are represented by the reference-species and buffer convention. Use a closed H2-bearing aqueous compartment; exclude cyanide and sulfide concentrations that poison accessible Ni sites. Commercial catalyst surface area must not be equated with a natural grain surface.

reactions.mechanism: Nickel activates H2 and hydrogenates the imine formed between oxaloacetate and ammonia. Competing direct carbonyl hydrogenation produces malate through rxn_015.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated oxaloacetate-to-aspartate conversion using the H2/Ni platform and found no reductive products without a metal catalyst. Their substrate-panel yields combine amino and hydroxy acids and are not an aspartate-specific yield. The integrated oxaloacetate/glyoxylate network produced only trace aspartate with Ni. Supported Ni is retained as an experimental benchmark; geological equivalence of natural Ni particles requires separate testing.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination over palladium

conditions.catalyst: Pd/C, 1 mol% Pd relative to ketoacid
conditions.other: Reported standard platform: 30 mM ketoacid, 150 mM NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 h. Use a separate anoxic H2-bearing compartment. The carbon support is a catalyst carrier, not a carbon feedstock. Cyanide-bearing solutions are not introduced. Environmental feasibility depends on an unusually Pd-enriched accessible surface and is not inferred from commercial Pd/C performance.

reactions.mechanism: Palladium dissociates H2 and reduces the oxaloacetate–ammonia imine, competing with carbonyl reduction and oxaloacetate decarboxylation.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated this terminal transformation and approximately 5% aspartate in their more complex Pd-containing oxaloacetate/glyoxylate network. That network yield is not assigned to the isolated-substrate conditions recorded here. Pd/C gives a useful mechanistic and selectivity benchmark, but palladium scarcity and the artificial support weaken its general geochemical applicability relative to its laboratory performance.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination over natural Fe–Ni meteoritic metal
agents: Ground natural iron meteorite containing approximately 11–18 mol% Ni

conditions.catalyst: Exposed metallic sites in ground Fe–Ni meteorite
conditions.other: Use the reported H2 platform as the operating baseline: 30 mM oxaloacetate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, up to 72 h. Meteorite mass, grain size and surface oxidation must be specified experimentally; they are not supplied quantitatively in the research summary. A proposed initial comparison normalizes powder additions to 10 mol% bulk Ni relative to substrate, without assuming that bulk Ni equals accessible catalytic Ni. Measure metal leaching and corrosion independently.

reactions.mechanism: Accessible meteoritic metal sites activate H2 and reduce the oxaloacetate-derived imine. Heterogeneous mineral composition and surface alteration govern the available active sites.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) showed that ground natural Fe–Ni meteorites catalyze ketoacid conversion to corresponding amino/hydroxy acids, including aspartate formation in the investigated substrate set. This supports a natural-metal implementation rather than requiring extraterrestrial synthesis of the product. The proposed bulk-Ni loading normalization is not a reported optimum, and supported-catalyst yields cannot be transferred to natural powders. Natural grain size, corrosion and sulfide passivation remain rate-controlling uncertainties.

reactions.name: Oxime-mediated oxaloacetate amination using hydroxylamine and iron
agents: Fe(0) powder as a consumed four-electron reductant

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm under an inert atmosphere
conditions.other: Proposed staged implementation: freshly supplied 5 mM oxaloacetate, 5–10 mM hydroxylamine, at least two molar equivalents of reactive Fe(0), pH screening from 5 to 7, and sampling at 5, 15, 60 and 180 min. These concentrations, pH values and sampling times are design values, not a reproduced published amination protocol. The supplied report establishes 343 K for the associated Fe(II) carbon network but does not fully specify the separate amination conditions. Do not run Fe(0)/hydroxylamine simultaneously with that upstream Fe(II) network.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine forms an oxime with oxaloacetate. Reduction of both the C=N and N–O functionality gives the amino acid. Two Fe(0)-to-Fe(II) oxidations provide the required four electrons; stoichiometric coefficients are inferred rather than encoded by repeated IDs.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) detected aspartate after hydroxylamine/Fe(0) treatment of their carbon network and supported the interpretation with corresponding ketoacid experiments. Thus the transformation is experimentally supported, while the fully numerical implementation proposed here requires validation against the primary protocol. Hydroxylamine sourcing remains uncertain. Kaur et al. (2024) identify interference between this amination system and Fe(II)-promoted carbon-network chemistry, motivating explicit staging rather than an unsupported one-pot claim.

reactions.name: Copper-assisted pyridoxamine transamination of oxaloacetate
agents: Cu(II), coordinated by the organic reactants and solution ligands

conditions.other: Reported representative screen: 10 mM oxaloacetate, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 7.8, approximately 1 h. Use a sulfide-free, anoxic aqueous microcompartment without Fe(0), H2-hydrogenation solids or cyanide. Nominal Cu addition does not mean 1 mM uncomplexed Cu2+. Track soluble and precipitated copper, and cool the product solution after the short reaction interval.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted Schiff-base formation and proton transfers move the amino group from pyridoxamine to oxaloacetate. Pyridoxal is the stoichiometric coproduct; pyridoxamine is not a catalytic nitrogen source unless separately regenerated.
reactions.reasoning: Harrison et al. (2023) reported approximately 5% aspartate within one hour with Cu(II), demonstrating trapping of oxaloacetate on a timescale competitive with decomposition. The supplied pyridoxamine inventory and its regeneration are outside this network boundary. Copper coordination and a local source of persistent Cu(II) must be established under anoxic conditions; anoxia alone does not establish that such a compartment exists. No molecular oxygen is consumed.

reactions.name: Nickel(II)-assisted pyridoxamine transamination of oxaloacetate

conditions.other: Use the reported representative metal screen: 10 mM oxaloacetate, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 7.8, approximately 1 h. Operate separately from Ni(0)/H2 reactions. Exclude sulfide-rich and phosphate-rich mixtures that can remove or redirect soluble metal species. Determine dissolved Ni and ligand-bound fractions instead of treating nominal addition as free-ion concentration.

reactions.mechanism: Ni(II) coordination promotes the pyridoxamine/oxaloacetate Schiff-base and proton-transfer sequence. Nitrogen transfer yields aspartate and pyridoxal without requiring H2 or oxidation of metallic nickel.
reactions.reasoning: Harrison et al. (2023) found measurable Ni(II)-promoted aspartate formation, although Cu(II) was superior under the screening conditions. No numerical Ni-specific yield is supplied in the research summary, so none is assigned. This is an experimentally supported alternative to Cu transamination and chemically distinct from Ni(0)-catalyzed hydrogenation. It avoids relying on the poorly defined near-neutral Al(III) implementation criticized in the earlier attempt, while still requiring metal-speciation measurements.

reactions.name: Formation of the glyoxylate–ammonia carbinolamine

conditions.temperature: 273 K for the reported isolation procedure
conditions.other: The reported preparation adds glyoxylic acid to concentrated ammonium acetate at 273 K. For a defined preliminary implementation, test 1 M glyoxylate in 2 M ammonium acetate near pH 7 for 1 h; these numerical concentration and time choices are proposed, not quoted experimental values. Confirm adduct identity and recovery before proceeding. Reconstitute isolated adduct to the 0.96 M loading needed in rxn_010. Cooling and isolation are separate operations, not assumed consequences of evaporation.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the glyoxylate carbonyl, forming alpha-hydroxyglycine without net water elimination.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) isolated alpha-hydroxyglycine in greater than 95% yield using concentrated ammonium acetate at 0 °C. That reported isolated yield does not establish the same conversion at the proposed concentrations or in an ambient surface pool. Reversible adduct formation, reagent concentration, cold-site availability and isolation efficiency must be assessed. No transition-metal catalyst or molecular oxygen is required.

reactions.name: Malonate coupling with alpha-hydroxyglycine

conditions.other: Reported conditions: 0.48 M malonate, two equivalents alpha-hydroxyglycine, 1 M bicarbonate, initial pH 7.2, five days. This corresponds to 0.96 M alpha-hydroxyglycine. Use an anoxic concentrated pool or microcompartment shielded from direct UV by sediment or water depth. Evaporation is only a proposed inventory-concentration mechanism; salt accumulation and adduct stability must be checked. No cyanide or transition-metal amination mixture is added.

reactions.mechanism: Malonate forms a carbon–carbon bond with the glyoxylate-derived nitrogen-bearing electrophile, with net water loss, producing beta-carboxyaspartate.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) directly established this condensation as the first step of their approximately 50%-overall-yield malonate-to-aspartate sequence. The transformation bypasses oxaloacetate, but the high malonate, adduct and bicarbonate concentrations and five-day residence time are substantial environmental requirements. The 50% value belongs to the combined condensation/decarboxylation sequence, not to this step alone.

reactions.name: Magnesium-promoted beta-carboxyaspartate decarboxylation

conditions.catalyst: Mg(II) decarboxylation promoter; catalytic turnover is not assumed
conditions.other: Reported sequential treatment: add one equivalent MgCl2 after the five-day condensation and heat at 333 K for five hours. Retain the preceding aqueous reaction mixture rather than inserting an unsupported purification step. The initial condensation pH is 7.2; follow pH and CO2 release during heating. Nominal Mg addition may exceed dissolved Mg because of carbonate complexation or precipitation. Cool afterward for product retention.

reactions.mechanism: Mg(II) coordination facilitates loss of one malonate-derived carboxyl group as CO2, producing the aspartate skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) obtained approximately 50% aspartate overall from malonate after the specified MgCl2/heating treatment. The experimentally tested sequence supports carrying the condensation mixture into this step. Geological operation still requires accessible Mg, the concentrated starting inventory and sufficiently limited side reactions. This Asp-forming branch does not require the peroxide chemistry used elsewhere in that paper.

reactions.name: Bucherer–Bergs conversion of oxaloacetate to N-carbamoylaspartate

conditions.other: Proposed ammonia/bicarbonate implementation: 5 mM freshly supplied oxaloacetate, 10–25 mM total cyanide, 50–150 mM total ammoniacal nitrogen, 0.1–0.5 M bicarbonate, pH 8–9. These concentrations and temperatures are design values, not a reconstruction of the optimized published Asp protocol. Monitor oxaloacetate capture within the first hour before allowing multiday conversion; the reported system includes experiments lasting approximately 14 days. Keep this compartment separate from all metal-catalyzed branches. Diamidophosphate is not silently treated as a catalyst or nitrogen source in this ammonia-fed implementation.

reactions.mechanism: A net, multistep Bucherer–Bergs sequence involving cyanide addition, nitrogen incorporation, carbamoyl/hydantoin chemistry, ring opening and decarboxylation yields N-carbamoylaspartate. CO2 is listed on both sides because its participation in carbamoylation and its release during decarboxylation cancel in the formal net species balance. The reaction is not represented as an elementary step or an experimentally resolved atom map.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support the oxaloacetate–cyanide–ammonia-source route through N-carbamoylaspartate. Their broader chemistry includes diamidophosphate; the supplied summary does not establish a complete optimized recipe for the ammonia-only implementation above. Consequently, that implementation is a proposed adaptation requiring validation, not a claimed reproduced yield. Carbonate participation is retained rather than omitted merely because it cancels from the net formula balance. Rapid initial trapping, cyanide retention and competition with rxn_014 are decisive bottlenecks.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic release of aspartate from N-carbamoylaspartate
agents: Acidic aqueous proton reservoir for the proposed hydrolysis implementation

conditions.catalyst: Aqueous acid in the proposed implementation
conditions.other: Proposed staged test: pH 1–2, sample over 1–14 days, then cool and equilibrate near pH 7–8 for aspartate accounting. These hydrolysis conditions are not specified in the supplied paper summary and are not asserted to reproduce its optimized conversion. Natural acidification would require a separate acidic pool or fluid input. Track N-carbamoylaspartate, aspartate and cyclic byproducts. The acidic-stage product is protonated according to local pH; the graph records its standardized aspartate reference form. No transfer into metal-containing compartments is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis removes the carbamoyl group, with its carbon and nitrogen ultimately released as CO2 and ammonia. Proton exchange gives the standardized aspartate formula used in the graph.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) report N-carbamoylaspartate-to-aspartate chemistry, supporting the endpoint transformation. The specific acid/temperature/time implementation proposed here is speculative because the supplied research does not provide its complete hydrolysis protocol. It requires direct kinetic validation: slow cleavage and competing cyclization could prevent useful Asp accumulation. No analytical-hydrolysis yield or environmental production rate is assumed. This explicitly identifies the remaining operational gap rather than presenting unspecified mild hydrolysis as established.

reactions.name: Competing oxaloacetate decarboxylation

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm to 5 bar, matched to the competing branch
conditions.other: Evaluate at each branch's actual pH, metal loading and buffer composition rather than using one universal decay constant. Source discussions describe oxaloacetate lifetimes on the order of hours under relevant mild conditions, with faster loss upon heating. Quantify oxaloacetate, pyruvate and aspartate in quenched early-time samples and through the productive reaction residence time. Fresh feed or immediate trapping is required; favorable productive flux is not inferred merely from including this sink.

reactions.mechanism: Beta-ketoacid decarboxylation releases CO2 and produces the enol of pyruvate, which tautomerizes to pyruvate.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019), Harrison et al. (2023) and Kaur et al. (2024) identify oxaloacetate instability as a central limitation on aspartate formation. Metal ions can alter the decay rate, so this uncatalyzed reference sink must be supplemented by measured rates in each actual reaction mixture. Its inclusion prevents the network from treating supplied oxaloacetate as indefinitely stable.

reactions.name: Competing hydrogenation of oxaloacetate to malate
agents: The Ni, Pd or natural Fe–Ni catalyst used in the corresponding H2 branch

conditions.catalyst: Matched to rxn_003, rxn_004 or rxn_005
conditions.other: Measure under the same 30 mM oxaloacetate, nominal 150 mM NH4HCO3, pH 8 and up-to-72-hour conditions as the corresponding reductive-amination branch. Lower-pH comparisons can assess the reported shift toward hydroxy-acid products. This node aggregates the common competing transformation, not a claim that the three catalysts have identical rates or selectivities.

reactions.mechanism: Surface-activated hydrogen reduces the keto group directly to an alcohol before productive imine reduction, consuming oxaloacetate as malate.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) report competition between amino-acid and hydroxy-acid formation and a pH-dependent shift in selectivity. Their combined product yields must therefore not be interpreted as aspartate yields. This sink accounts for a chemically supported loss of immediate Asp precursor without introducing an unsupported upstream regeneration cycle.

pathways.name: FeS–Fe(0) reductive amination
pathways.description: Supplied oxaloacetate and ammonia are converted directly to aspartate by preactivated FeS containing consumed Fe(0). The reported 64% conversion applies to the specified laboratory benchmark, not to a complete environmental synthesis.

pathways.name: Unsupported Fe(0) reductive amination
pathways.description: The same supplied carbon and nitrogen precursors are reduced using exposed metallic iron without a sulfide scaffold. This experimentally supported material alternative has poorer selectivity and requires its own kinetic characterization.

pathways.name: Supported Ni/H2 reductive amination
pathways.description: Oxaloacetate and ammonia undergo hydrogen-driven amination on supported Ni. This operational pathway is distinguished from P4 and P5 by the catalyst material and from P8 by the oxidation state and mechanism of nickel.

pathways.name: Pd/C–H2 reductive amination
pathways.description: Pd/C catalyzes oxaloacetate imine hydrogenation. It is included as a demonstrated alternative and selectivity benchmark, with palladium availability and support realism explicitly limiting geological interpretation.

pathways.name: Natural Fe–Ni metal–H2 reductive amination
pathways.description: Natural meteoritic metal provides the hydrogenation surface. The aspartate is formed in the aqueous reaction compartment, not assumed to have been delivered already synthesized from space.

pathways.name: Hydroxylamine/Fe(0) oxime-reduction route
pathways.description: Supplied oxaloacetate reacts through an oxime-derived intermediate and is reduced to aspartate by Fe(0). The transformation is experimentally supported, while the specified preliminary operating window requires validation. Hydroxylamine supply and upstream-network incompatibility remain explicit limitations.

pathways.name: Cu(II)/pyridoxamine transamination
pathways.description: Pyridoxamine transfers its amino group to oxaloacetate in a short Cu-assisted reaction, producing pyridoxal. Pyridoxamine is consumed rather than silently regenerated, and the compartment is isolated from cyanide, sulfide and strong reductants.

pathways.name: Ni(II)/pyridoxamine transamination
pathways.description: Soluble ligand-bound Ni(II) promotes the experimentally observed transamination alternative. It is weaker than Cu under the reported screen and is not equated with metallic Ni/H2 chemistry or assigned an unsupported quantitative yield.

pathways.name: Glyoxylate–ammonia–malonate assembly
pathways.description: Glyoxylate and ammonia form alpha-hydroxyglycine; malonate coupling gives beta-carboxyaspartate; Mg-promoted decarboxylation releases aspartate. The laboratory sequence bypasses oxaloacetate and external reductants, but requires cold adduct preparation, high concentrations, a five-day condensation and staged warming.

pathways.name: Cyanide/Bucherer–Bergs–carbamoylaspartate route
pathways.description: Oxaloacetate is diverted through cyanide/ammonia/carbonate chemistry to N-carbamoylaspartate, followed by hydrolytic release of aspartate. The route family and intermediate are literature-supported; the fully specified ammonia-only and acid-hydrolysis implementations are proposed adaptations, not claimed reproductions of the optimized published protocol. This is the least operationally resolved pathway in the network and remains separate from metal chemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kitadai et al. (2019, Science Advances) directly support OAA-to-Asp conversion with partially electroreduced FeS containing Fe(0). The equation correctly treats metallic iron as a consumed reductant. The reported 64% Asp yield is strong evidence for this transformation, but the submitted reaction does not specify the conditions or preparation needed to reproduce that result. The declared OAA inventory is consistent with the stated precursor-to-target scope.
suggestions: Attach the published benchmark conditions to the reaction record if intended: 5 mM OAA, 0.5 M ammonia, pH 9.6, 23–25 °C and 48 hours.

Document the FeS–Fe(0) material loading and preparation, including the reported electroreduction at approximately −0.7 V versus SHE for seven days. Distinguish this demonstrated preparation from any proposed environmental generation mechanism.
Compare Asp formation with rxn_014 under the actual chosen conditions before making productivity claims.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Unsupported Fe(0)-driven reductive amination is supported by Kitadai et al. (2019). The stoichiometry is valid, and Asp formation is credible. The important distinction from P1 is experimentally observed competition from OAA decarboxylation and subsequent pyruvate chemistry, not a different overall reaction mechanism. Including rxn_014 appropriately acknowledges this loss channel, although no rates or unsupported-iron-specific selectivity are supplied.
suggestions: Specify the unsupported iron loading, particle size, surface condition, ammonia concentration, pH, temperature and reaction time.
Use unsupported-Fe-specific Asp measurements rather than assigning the FeS–Fe(0) system's 64% yield to this pathway.
For a quantitative network model, account for pyruvate-derived products and iron passivation as well as Asp production.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024, Chem) experimentally support supported-Ni/H2 reductive amination of OAA. The net equation is chemically and stoichiometrically sound. Catalyst-dependent competition with malate formation is appropriately represented elsewhere by rxn_015. The literature's combined amino-plus-hydroxy-acid yield ranges are not Asp-specific yields, and the submitted network does not establish an operating pressure, catalyst loading or aqueous composition.
suggestions: If adopting the published standard protocol, record 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 22 °C, 5 bar H2, 72 hours and 10 mol% supported Ni.
Identify the support and catalyst preparation explicitly; do not assume another Ni-bearing material has equivalent activity.
Attach OAA-specific Asp and malate measurements and assign rxn_015 to the same H2/Ni compartment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Pd/C–H2 implementation is supported by Kaur et al. (2024), and the balanced reductive-amination equation produces the correct target. Its inclusion is justified as an operational catalyst alternative, without treating it as an independent mechanistic family. Experimental catalyst availability and environmental occurrence are separate questions; neither a particular natural setting nor a reproducible operating protocol is established by the current reaction entry.
suggestions: Specify the Pd/C formulation, loading and hydrogenation conditions; the supplied research describes a standard benchmark using 1 mol% Pd, pH 8, 22 °C and 5 bar H2.
Distinguish isolated-OAA results from the approximately 5% Asp obtained in the more complex OAA–glyoxylate network.
Report OAA-specific selectivity rather than applying the across-substrate 52–88% combined-product range to Asp.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated amino-acid formation using ground Fe–Ni meteorites, including Asp from OAA. Representing H2 as the reductant is consistent with that implementation. However, natural provenance does not establish the activity of an unspecified metal sample: composition, exposed metallic surface and preparation matter. The route is credible, but its environmental and quantitative performance remain conditional on a characterized material and stated conditions.
suggestions: Identify the tested material or a characterized equivalent, including Ni content, particle size, metallic fraction and oxidation state of the exposed surface.
Specify catalyst loading, H2 pressure, pH, temperature and residence time, and attach meteorite-specific Asp measurements.
If proposing an environmental implementation, justify the required exposed surface area and H2 availability without assuming that laboratory-ground material represents untreated grains.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019, Nature) support hydroxylamine/Fe(0)-mediated formation of Asp. Oxime formation followed by reduction is plausible. The deterministic check establishes that rxn_006 is balanceable with two Fe atoms, three protons and two waters; this is not a conservation violation. Declaring hydroxylamine supplied and separating this compartment from incompatible carbon-network chemistry appropriately limits the claim. The actual amination protocol remains unspecified.
suggestions: Write the explicit stoichiometry: C4H4O5 + H3NO + 2 Fe + 3 H+ -> C4H6NO4^- + 2 Fe^2+ + 2 H2O.
Provide the amination-specific pH, temperature, iron loading, atmosphere, addition sequence and duration rather than assuming all conditions of the upstream Fe(II) carbon-network experiment apply.
Identify the reaction as a lumped oxime-formation/reduction sequence and document competing hydroxylamine consumption where quantitative performance is claimed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Harrison et al. (2023, Life) directly support Cu(II)-assisted pyridoxamine transamination of OAA, with approximately 5% Asp formation within one hour under reported conditions. Pyridoxamine consumption and pyridoxal formation are correctly represented. Pyridoxamine regeneration is unnecessary for the declared supplied-inventory, noncontinuous pathway. The missing operating conditions and dissolved-copper specification prevent stronger environmental confidence.
suggestions: Attach a condition-specific experimental record. The supplied research describes a representative screen with 10 mM OAA, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 7.8, 70 °C and 1 mM metal ion.
Document copper availability and speciation in the actual buffer and verify that the selected condition set corresponds to the cited Asp measurement.
Compare transamination and OAA decarboxylation on the same timescale without extrapolating the measured endpoint to sustained production.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied account of Harrison et al. (2023) reports measurable Ni(II)-promoted Asp formation, supporting this as a chemically valid transamination implementation. Its weaker screening performance does not invalidate target achievement. Nevertheless, the Cu-specific yield and rate cannot be assigned to Ni(II), and the reaction entry lacks a Ni-specific protocol and product measurement. Pyridoxamine-to-pyridoxal bookkeeping is sound.
suggestions: Attach the Ni(II)-specific conditions, Asp measurement and comparison with the no-metal control.
Specify dissolved Ni(II) loading and effective speciation in the bicarbonate/pyridoxamine mixture.
Use Ni-specific kinetic data when comparing rxn_008 against rxn_014; do not infer its performance from the Cu-assisted pathway.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Springsteen et al. (2018, Nature Communications) directly support the alpha-hydroxyglycine/beta-carboxyaspartate sequence and approximately 50% overall Asp yield from malonate. All three equations conserve atoms and charge, and the intermediates are appropriately identified. The principal gap is operational: the reaction entries do not specify the distinct adduct-formation, condensation and Mg(II)-promoted decarboxylation conditions. The Biochemical-to-Surface labels alone do not establish how the stages are implemented.
suggestions: Document cold adduct preparation in concentrated ammonium acetate separately from the condensation benchmark: approximately 480 mM malonate, two equivalents alpha-hydroxyglycine, 1 M bicarbonate, initial pH 7.2, 23 °C and five days.
Specify the final MgCl2 addition and heating stage; the supplied study reports one equivalent MgCl2 followed by 60 °C for five hours.
State whether the stages use one aqueous compartment with scheduled additions and heating or an actual transfer, and document dilution, retention and dissolved Mg(II) availability accordingly.
Treat the reported concentrations as conditions requiring implementation, not as evidence that the supplied feedstocks spontaneously accumulate together.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Pulletikurti et al. (2022, Nature Chemistry) support the OAA–cyanide/N-carbamoylaspartate route family. Both submitted equations are balanced; CO2 appearing on both sides of rxn_012 is not a conservation error. However, rxn_012 compresses multistep Bucherer–Bergs chemistry, while rxn_013 supplies no conditions establishing hydrolysis to free Asp. N-carbamoyl hydrolysis cannot be assumed to proceed adequately merely because water and a surface environment are present. The route is plausible but less completely specified than the other alternatives.
suggestions: Identify rxn_012 explicitly as a lumped net transformation and document the OAA-specific intervening chemistry, including the role and atom provenance of cyanide and carbonate/CO2.
Provide the actual ammonia source, concentrations, pH, temperature, staging and duration from the Asp-specific experimental protocol.
Clarify whether DAP or another additive is required for this particular branch; its use elsewhere in the broader study does not establish that it is mandatory here.
For rxn_013, supply condition-specific evidence for free Asp formation and distinguish hydrolysis from retention as N-carbamoylaspartate or diversion into pyrimidine-related products.
Retain the stated separation from metal-catalyzed compartments; no cyanide–metal compatibility assumption is needed.

evaluation.network_feedback: This is a chemically credible, connected precursor-to-aspartate alternative-pathway network, but it does not reach the 0.90 network-approval threshold. Molecule IDs are consistent, the graph has no isolated subgraphs, and the deterministic check establishes conservation for all 15 reactions. rxn_006 needs only the small explicit coefficients reported by the checker. Neutral organic-acid reference formulas, buffer-exchange protons and net-minus-one Asp are mutually consistent conventions; free Fe(II) remains an acknowledged simplification of downstream speciation. Literature alignment is strong at the route-selection level, although the submitted reaction records lack individual citations and condition-linked evidence. The main network-wide limitation is environmental specification: Biochemical and Surface do not define temperature, pressure, pH, aqueous composition, catalyst preparation or catalyst availability.
